cues: Welcome to Claude and MCP — the complete visual guide, with a special focus on finance.
Prepared by Sara Salem.
In this video, you'll learn what the Model Context Protocol is, how it works under the hood, how to connect it to Claude, and how financial teams use it to work faster and smarter.
Let's start with a problem. On its own, an AI model is isolated. It can't see your live market data, your company's databases, or your documents.

Before MCP, every connection had to be built by hand. Every AI app needed a custom integration for every data source. With many apps and many sources, that quickly becomes a tangled web — N times M integrations.
MCP changes that. Each app implements the protocol once, and each data source implements it once. Now everything can talk to everything — with just N plus M.
Less custom code, less maintenance, and a lot more possibilities.
So, what exactly is MCP?
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It's an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI assistants to the systems where data lives.
A popular way to describe it: MCP is like a USB-C port for AI. One standard plug, that works with many different devices.
Through MCP, Claude can connect to databases, business tools, file systems, and financial data platforms — all in one consistent way.
And because it's open, it has been adopted across the industry, with thousands of MCP servers available today.
Let's look at the architecture. MCP has a few key building blocks.
First, the host. That's the AI application you use — like the Claude app, Claude Desktop, or Claude Code.
Inside the host, an MCP client manages one connection to each server.
The client and the server talk using JSON-RPC messages. Locally, they communicate over standard input and output. Remotely, they use streamable HTTP.
The MCP server is a lightweight program that exposes specific capabilities — for example, a server for your data warehouse, or for a market data provider.
And behind the server sits the real data source: a database, an API, or a document store.
MCP servers offer three core building blocks, called primitives.
Tools are actions Claude can take — functions like get stock price, or run a query. Claude decides when to call them, and you stay in control.
Resources are data Claude can read — such as files, database records, or reports — to add context to the conversation.
Prompts are reusable templates that guide Claude through common workflows, like a monthly variance analysis.
And in the other direction, clients can offer features to servers too — such as asking the user for extra input, which is called elicitation.
Let's see what happens behind the scenes, when Claude calls a tool.
First, the client and the server shake hands with an initialize message, and agree on which capabilities they support.
Next, the client asks the server for its list of tools. Each tool comes with a name, a description, and an input schema.
When Claude decides to use a tool, the client sends a tools call request — here, asking for a company's latest quarterly revenue.
The server runs the request against the real data source, and sends back the result. Claude then uses it in its answer.
Now, how do you connect MCP servers to Claude? There are four main ways.
In the Claude apps, open Settings, then Connectors. Browse the directory, or add a custom connector with its URL, and sign in securely.
In Claude Desktop, you can install desktop extensions with one click, or run local servers on your own computer.
In Claude Code, a single command — claude mcp add — connects a server right from your terminal.
And developers can use the MCP connector in the Claude API, to attach remote servers directly to their requests.
Now let's focus on finance — one of the areas where MCP makes the biggest difference.
Without MCP, analysts jump between terminals, spreadsheets, PDFs, and databases. They copy and paste numbers by hand, which is slow, and easy to get wrong.
With MCP, Claude connects directly to trusted financial data. It pulls the latest figures, combines sources in seconds, and shows where every number came from.
That means less time gathering data, and more time for analysis and judgment.
Anthropic's Claude for Financial Services brings together connectors to leading financial data providers. Here are the main categories.
Market and company data — from providers like S&P Global, FactSet, and LSEG — for prices, fundamentals, and estimates.
Private market data — such as PitchBook — for deals, private companies, and funds.
Research and ratings — from sources like Morningstar and Moody's.
Fundamentals and earnings data, from specialists like Daloopa, together with earnings call transcripts.
Your own data platforms — like Snowflake and Databricks — where your internal financial data lives.
And document platforms, such as Box, for data rooms, contracts, and reports. Availability depends on your plan, and on your subscriptions with each provider.
Let's follow a real-world example. An analyst asks Claude: build a comparable companies analysis for three software firms.
Step one: Claude understands the request, and plans which data it needs.
Step two: it calls market data tools through MCP, to pull revenue, margins, and valuation multiples.
Step three: it queries the company's own data warehouse, for internal estimates and notes.
Step four: it builds the analysis — for example, a formatted Excel workbook with live formulas.
And step five: it delivers a clear summary, with sources cited, ready for the analyst to review.
Here are some of the most powerful ways financial teams use Claude with MCP.
Equity research, with fast company profiles and peer comparisons. Financial modeling, from DCF models to scenario analysis. And due diligence, reviewing data rooms in a fraction of the time.
Portfolio monitoring, with alerts and summaries of what changed. Earnings analysis, turning long transcripts into key insights. And risk and compliance, checking documents against policies.
Plus FP and A, for budgets and variance analysis. And client reporting, with clear and consistent reports for every client.
In finance, trust and security come first. MCP and Claude are designed with several layers of protection.
Layer one: access control. Remote servers use secure sign-in, like OAuth, and Claude only sees the data your account is allowed to see.
Layer two: human in the loop. You can review and approve tool calls, especially actions that change data.
Layer three: audit and governance. Organizations can control which connectors are available, and keep records for compliance.
Together, these layers help keep sensitive financial data safe, while still unlocking the power of AI.
Want to build your own MCP server? It's simpler than you might think. Here's an example in Python.
First, you create a server, and give it a name — here, a finance data server.
Then you define a tool, using a simple decorator. The function name, the description, and the typed parameters tell Claude what the tool does, and how to call it.
Inside the function, you connect to your real data source — such as your pricing database, or an internal API.
Finally, you run the server. Connect it to Claude, and your tool is ready to use in any conversation.
Before we finish, here are six best practices for using MCP in finance.
One: start with read-only access, and expand permissions only when needed.
Two: follow least privilege. Give each connector only the data it truly requires.
Three: use official or trusted servers, from providers you already work with.
Four: always verify key numbers, and check the sources that Claude cites.
Five: keep a human in the loop for important decisions. Claude supports analysts — it doesn't replace their judgment.
And six: monitor and review usage regularly, to stay aligned with your compliance requirements.
Let's recap in one line: connect, analyze, decide.
MCP gives Claude a secure, standard way to reach your financial data — so your team can move from raw data to real insight, faster.
